title: C#
description: Learn C# from scratch: output, variables, input, decisions, loops, methods, arrays and strings, classes, recursion, sorting and searching; then exceptions, interfaces, generics, LINQ, records, delegates and events, graphs with BFS, dynamic programming, iterators with yield and Dijkstra's algorithm. The same language used in games (Unity), Windows apps and servers.

cs-01.title: Hello, world!
cs-01.theory:
# Your first C# program

C# (pronounced "C sharp") is a **compiled**, **strongly typed** language created by Microsoft. Before running, the compiler reads all of your code and checks that everything makes sense. If there is a typo, the program doesn't even start: you get a message telling you the line of the problem. This seems annoying at first, but it is a big help: many errors are caught before the program runs.

## Writing to the screen

To show text, we use `Console.WriteLine`:

```csharp
Console.WriteLine("Olá, mundo!");
```

Let's understand each piece:

- `Console` is the **class** that represents the terminal (the text screen).
- `.WriteLine` is a **method** of that class: it writes the text and moves to the next line.
- The text between double quotes `"..."` is a **string** (a sequence of characters).
- The `;` at the end finishes the statement. In C#, **every statement ends with a semicolon**.

There is also `Console.Write`, which writes **without** moving to the next line:

```csharp
Console.Write("Olá, ");
Console.WriteLine("mundo!");
// result: Olá, mundo!
```

## Top-level statements

In modern C# (since version 9) you can write statements directly in the file, with no "ceremony". Behind the scenes the compiler creates a class and a `Main` method for you. In the next lessons we will see the full structure; for now, enjoy the simplicity.

Statements run **from top to bottom**, one after the other. The order of the lines is the order of what appears on the screen.

## Comments

Everything after `//` until the end of the line is ignored by the compiler. Use comments to explain the **why** of the code:

```csharp
// This is a comment
Console.WriteLine("Isto aparece"); // comment at the end of the line
```

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the `;` at the end: the compiler reports `; expected`.
- Using single quotes for text: `'Olá'` is an error. Single quotes are for **a single character** (`'A'`).
- Writing `console.writeline`: C# is case sensitive. The correct form is `Console.WriteLine`.
- Spaces and accents inside the quotes are part of the text: the checker compares the output **exactly**.

cs-02.title: Variables and types
cs-02.theory:
# Storing values in variables

In the previous lesson we wrote fixed texts. Real programs work with **data** that changes, and for that we use **variables**: names that hold a value in memory.

In C# every variable has a **type**, and that type never changes. That is what "strongly typed" means:

```csharp
int idade = 20;          // whole number
double altura = 1.75;    // number with decimal places
string nome = "Ana";     // text
bool estudante = true;   // true or false
char inicial = 'A';      // a single character
```

The general form is `type name = value;`. Once declared, the variable can receive new values **of the same type**:

```csharp
idade = 21;        // ok
idade = "vinte";   // COMPILE ERROR: string is not int
```

## Why types?

The type tells the compiler how much memory to reserve and which operations make sense. Adding two `int` is arithmetic; "adding" two `string` is concatenating. If you try something that makes no sense, the error shows up **before** the program runs, not in the middle of your user's game.

## The var keyword

You can let the compiler infer the type from the initial value:

```csharp
var pontos = 100;   // the compiler understands: int
```

The variable still has a fixed type (`int`); `var` only saves typing.

## Showing variables: interpolation

To mix text and values, put a `$` before the quotes and the variables between braces:

```csharp
Console.WriteLine($"Nome: {nome}");
Console.WriteLine($"Daqui a 5 anos: {idade + 5}");
Console.WriteLine($"Altura: {altura:F2}");
```

Inside the braces there can be any expression. The `:F2` formats the number with **exactly 2 decimal places** (`1.7` becomes `1.70`). In this course the decimal separator is always the **dot**: EasyCreator runs your program with the "invariant" culture. On a computer set to Portuguese, the same code would show `1,70`, and `double.Parse` would expect a comma in the input.

One detail: a `bool` is shown as `True` or `False`, with a capital first letter.

## Common mistakes

- Using a variable before giving it a value: the compiler complains.
- Writing `1,75` instead of `1.75` in the code: in C# the decimal in code is always written with a dot.
- Forgetting the `$` before the quotes: the braces appear literally on the screen.
- Variable names can't contain spaces or start with a number. Use `camelCase`: `alturaEmMetros`.

cs-03.title: Input and arithmetic
cs-03.theory:
# Reading data and doing math

So far the values were fixed in the code. Now the program will **read** data from whoever uses it.

## Console.ReadLine

`Console.ReadLine()` reads **a whole line** of input and returns a `string`:

```csharp
string nome = Console.ReadLine();
```

**Important:** here in the course the checker types the input **automatically** for your program, one line at a time. So **do not** write messages like "Type a number:" before reading: they would appear in the output and the test would fail.

## Converting text to a number

What comes from the keyboard is always text. `"5" + "3"` gives `"53"`, not `8`! To do math, convert:

```csharp
int a = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());
double preco = double.Parse(Console.ReadLine());
```

If the text is not a valid number, `int.Parse` throws an error and the program stops. In the next lessons we will see how to deal with that; for now, trust that the input is valid.

## Arithmetic operators

```csharp
int a = 17, b = 5;
Console.WriteLine(a + b);  // 22
Console.WriteLine(a - b);  // 12
Console.WriteLine(a * b);  // 85
Console.WriteLine(a / b);  // 3   (integer division!)
Console.WriteLine(a % b);  // 2   (remainder of the division)
```

The trickiest point: **dividing two `int` gives an `int`**. The decimal part is simply discarded (truncated toward zero). So `-17 / 5` gives `-3` and `-17 % 5` gives `-2`: the remainder has the sign of the dividend.

To get a division with decimals, at least one side must be a `double`:

```csharp
double media = (a + b) / 2.0;      // 2.0 is a double
double media2 = (double)(a + b) / 2; // explicit conversion (cast)
```

The `(double)` in front is a **cast**: it converts the value to another type.

## Precedence

As in math, `*`, `/` and `%` come before `+` and `-`. Use parentheses when in doubt: `(a + b) / 2` is very different from `a + b / 2`.

## Common mistakes

- Adding strings thinking they add numbers: convert with `int.Parse` first.
- Computing an average with `(a + b) / 2` using `int`: the decimal part disappears.
- Forgetting to format: use `{media:F2}` to always get 2 decimal places.

cs-06.title: Methods
cs-06.theory:
# Organizing code into methods

As programs grow, repeating the same snippet in several places becomes a problem: a bug has to be fixed in every copy. The solution is to give a **name** to a piece of code: a **method** (in other languages, a "function").

## The full structure of a program

So far we have used top-level statements. Behind the scenes, every C# program looks like this:

```csharp
using System;

class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Começa aqui");
    }
}
```

- `class Program` groups the code (classes are the subject of lesson 8).
- `static void Main()` is the **entry point**: the first method that runs.
- `using System;` lets you write `Console` instead of `System.Console` (in modern .NET it is already implicit).

## Declaring a method

```csharp
static int Quadrado(int x)
{
    return x * x;
}
```

- `static`: belongs to the class, with no need to create an object (we'll see this in lesson 8).
- `int` before the name: the **return type**. Use `void` when the method returns nothing.
- `(int x)`: the **parameters**, each with its type.
- `return`: returns the value and **ends** the method right away.

Calling it: `int q = Quadrado(5); // 25`.

## Why methods?

1. **Reuse**: write once, use many times.
2. **Readability**: `if (EhPrimo(n))` explains the intent better than ten lines of loop.
3. **Testing**: a small method is easy to check in isolation.

## Early return

A `return` in the middle of the method is an elegant way to handle special cases: as soon as it runs, the method ends and the rest isn't even executed.

```csharp
static string Sinal(int n)
{
    if (n < 0) return "negativo";   // exits here
    if (n == 0) return "zero";       // or here
    return "positivo";
}
```

## Example: prime number

A number is **prime** if it is greater than 1 and is divisible only by 1 and itself. We don't need to test all divisors up to `n`: if `n = a * b`, one of the two is at most the square root of `n`. So it is enough to test `d` while `d * d <= n`. For `n = 1 000 003` that is about 1000 tests instead of a million. Thinking about **how much work** the algorithm does is the beginning of complexity analysis (lesson 10).

## Scope

Variables declared inside a method only exist inside it. Parameters receive **copies** of the values (for types like `int`):

```csharp
static bool EhPar(int n)
{
    if (n < 0) n = -n;   // changes only the copy
    return n % 2 == 0;
}
```

If `x` is -4, calling `EhPar(x)` does not change the caller's `x`: it is still -4.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the `return` in some path of a non-`void` method: compile error "not all code paths return a value".
- Forgetting `static` when calling a method from `Main`.
- Treating 0, 1 and negatives as primes: they are **not**.

cs-07.title: Arrays and strings
cs-07.theory:
# Collections of values and text manipulation

In lesson 5 we read several numbers, but each one was forgotten right after being used. To **store** many values we use **arrays**, and to work with text we use the `string` methods.

## Arrays

An array has a fixed size and all elements of the same type:

```csharp
int[] notas = new int[3];       // [0, 0, 0]
notas[0] = 8;
int[] primos = { 2, 3, 5, 7 };  // already with values
Console.WriteLine(primos.Length); // 4
Console.WriteLine(primos[3]);     // 7
```

Indices go from `0` to `Length - 1`. Accessing `primos[4]` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`: C# **checks** every access, which prevents silent bugs (in C that would corrupt memory).

To walk through it, use `for` (when you need the index) or `foreach` (when you only need the values):

```csharp
foreach (int p in primos)
    Console.WriteLine(p);
```

If the size needs to vary, use `List<int>`, which grows with `Add`. We'll see more in lesson 8.

## Strings

A `string` behaves like a read-only array of `char`:

```csharp
string s = "Olá";
Console.WriteLine(s.Length);   // 3
Console.WriteLine(s[0]);       // O
Console.WriteLine(s.ToUpper()); // OLÁ
```

Strings are **immutable**: `ToUpper()` does not change `s`, it returns a new string.

## Split and Join

`Split` breaks a text into pieces; `string.Join` does the reverse:

```csharp
string frase = "  um   dois tres ";
string[] palavras = frase.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
// ["um", "dois", "tres"]
Console.WriteLine(string.Join("-", palavras)); // um-dois-tres
```

Without `RemoveEmptyEntries`, repeated spaces would produce empty pieces (`""`) and the word count would be wrong.

`Array.Reverse(palavras)` reverses the array **in place** (it modifies the array itself).

## Empty line and null

If the input ends, `Console.ReadLine()` returns `null`. A safe way to read is:

```csharp
string linha = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
```

The `??` operator uses the right-hand value when the left-hand one is `null`.

## Common mistakes

- A loop with `i <= arr.Length`: overflows the index on the last iteration.
- Comparing strings thinking `ToUpper()` changed the original.
- Concatenating strings inside very large loops: each `+` creates a new string. For many pieces, prefer `string.Join` or `StringBuilder`.
- On a length tie, deciding which word stays: with `>` (and not `>=`) you keep the **first**.

cs-09.title: Recursion
cs-09.theory:
# Methods that call themselves

In lesson 6 we saw that a method can call another. It can also call **itself**: this is **recursion**. The idea is to solve a big problem using the solution of the **same problem, only smaller**.

## The two required parts

```csharp
static long Fatorial(int n)
{
    if (n == 0) return 1;          // base case
    return n * Fatorial(n - 1);    // recursive step
}
```

1. **Base case**: a simple situation that answers directly, without recursion.
2. **Recursive step**: calls the method with a **smaller** input, getting closer to the base case.

If the base case is missing (or the input doesn't shrink), the calls never stop and the program dies with `StackOverflowException`.

## What happens inside

Each call gets its own space on the **call stack**, with its own variables. `Fatorial(3)` waits for `Fatorial(2)`, which waits for `Fatorial(1)`, which waits for `Fatorial(0)`. When the base case returns 1, the results "come back" multiplying: 1, 1, 2, 6.

The stack is limited (about 1 MB per thread in .NET), so recursions with millions of levels overflow. For simple linear problems, a loop is usually better; recursion shines when the problem **divides** naturally: trees, folders inside folders, divide and conquer (lesson 10).

## Tower of Hanoi

Three pegs (A, B, C) and `n` discs of different sizes stacked on A, from the largest (at the bottom) to the smallest. Goal: move all of them to C, moving **one disc at a time** and **never** placing a larger disc on a smaller one.

It seems hard to program with loops, but recursion solves it in three steps. To move `n` discs from `origem` to `destino`:

1. move the top `n - 1` discs from `origem` to the `auxiliar` peg (using `destino` as support);
2. move disc `n` (the largest) from `origem` to `destino`;
3. move the `n - 1` discs from `auxiliar` to `destino` (using `origem` as support).

The base case is `n == 0`: there is nothing to move.

```csharp
static void Hanoi(int n, char origem, char destino, char auxiliar)
{
    if (n == 0) return;
    Hanoi(n - 1, origem, auxiliar, destino);
    Console.WriteLine($"Mova o disco {n} de {origem} para {destino}");
    Hanoi(n - 1, auxiliar, destino, origem);
}
```

Trust the recursion: when writing step 1, **assume** that `Hanoi(n - 1, ...)` already works. This "leap of faith" is the same reasoning as **mathematical induction**.

## How many moves?

Let `M(n)` be the number of moves: `M(0) = 0` and `M(n) = 2·M(n-1) + 1`. This gives `M(n) = 2^n - 1`. With 20 discs, more than a million moves; with 64, even making one move per second, it would take about 585 billion years, more than 40 times the age of the universe. It is an example of **exponential** growth, O(2^n).

In C#, `1 << n` computes `2^n` for integers (it shifts the bit 1 left by `n` positions). With `int` this holds up to n = 30; for larger exponents use `1L << n` (`long`, up to n = 62).

## Common mistakes

- Swapping the order of the pegs in the recursive calls.
- Forgetting the base case.
- Using `Math.Pow`, which returns `double`, when you want an exact integer.

cs-11.title: Exceptions: handling errors
cs-11.theory:
# Exceptions

Real programs receive bad data: text where a number was expected, divisions by zero, files that don't exist. In C#, when something goes wrong at run time, the code **throws an exception**: an object that describes the problem. If nobody **catches** it, the program stops with an error message. Catching exceptions lets you react to the problem and carry on.

## try and catch

```csharp
try
{
    int x = int.Parse("abc");      // throws FormatException
    Console.WriteLine("never gets here");
}
catch (FormatException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("That is not a number.");
}
```

As soon as an exception is thrown inside the `try`, the rest of the block is **skipped** and C# looks for a matching `catch`.

## Several catches: from the most specific to the most general

Exceptions form a class hierarchy. `DivideByZeroException` and `OverflowException` are kinds of `ArithmeticException`, which is a kind of `Exception`. C# tests the `catch` blocks **in order** and uses the first one that fits, so the specific ones come first:

```csharp
catch (DivideByZeroException) { ... }
catch (OverflowException) { ... }
catch (Exception e) { Console.WriteLine(e.Message); }  // anything else
```

Some common exceptions:

| Exception | When it happens |
|---|---|
| `FormatException` | `int.Parse("abc")` |
| `OverflowException` | `int.Parse("99999999999")`, or a `checked` calculation that overflows |
| `DivideByZeroException` | **integer** division by zero |
| `IndexOutOfRangeException` | `v[10]` in an array of 10 |
| `NullReferenceException` | using a `null` variable |
| `KeyNotFoundException` | a missing key in a dictionary |

## checked: overflow becomes an exception

By default, an `int` that goes past 2147483647 silently **wraps around** and becomes negative. Inside `checked(...)`, the overflow throws `OverflowException`:

```csharp
int a = 100000;
int r = checked(a * a);   // OverflowException instead of a wrong number
```

## Throwing your own exceptions

```csharp
throw new ArgumentException($"operador desconhecido '{op}'");
```

The text becomes the `Message` property, which whoever catches it can show.

## finally

A `finally` block **always** runs, with or without an exception. It is used to release resources (closing files, connections), making sure that happens even when something fails.

## TryParse: when the error is expected

Exceptions are for **exceptional** situations. If invalid data is common, `int.TryParse(text, out int value)` returns `false` without throwing anything, and it is faster. Use exceptions to separate the normal path from error handling, not to control ordinary loops.

## Common mistakes

- An empty `catch (Exception)` that "swallows" every error and hides bugs.
- Putting the general `catch` before the specific ones (the compiler complains).
- Forgetting that dividing a `double` by zero does **not** throw: it gives `∞` or `NaN`.

cs-14.title: LINQ: queries over collections
cs-14.theory:
# LINQ

A good part of programming is asking questions about collections of data: "what are the total sales per category?", "who sold the most?", "which products went over a thousand?". With loops, each question becomes several lines of code. **LINQ** (*Language Integrated Query*) lets you write these questions **declaratively**: you say **what** you want, not **how** to go through the data.

## The basic operators

They all come from `System.Linq` and work on any `IEnumerable<T>` (arrays, lists, dictionaries...). They receive **lambdas**: short functions written as `x => expression`.

```csharp
int[] v = { 5, 3, 8, 1, 9 };

v.Where(x => x > 4)            // filters: 5 8 9
v.Select(x => x * 10)          // transforms: 50 30 80 10 90
v.OrderBy(x => x)              // sorts: 1 3 5 8 9
v.OrderByDescending(x => x)    // 9 8 5 3 1
v.Sum()  v.Max()  v.Count()    // aggregate: 26, 9, 5
v.Count(x => x % 2 == 1)       // counts the ones that match: 4
v.First(x => x > 6)            // the first one that matches: 8
v.Any(x => x > 100)            // is there any? false
```

The operations **chain**, each one receiving the result of the previous one:

```csharp
var top = v.Where(x => x > 2).OrderBy(x => x).Take(2);   // 3 5
```

## Grouping: GroupBy

`GroupBy` splits the elements into groups with the same **key**. Each group has the `Key` property and is itself a collection:

```csharp
var porCategoria = vendas
    .GroupBy(v => v.Categoria)
    .Select(g => new { Categoria = g.Key, Total = g.Sum(v => v.Valor), Vendas = g.Count() })
    .OrderByDescending(x => x.Total)
    .ThenBy(x => x.Categoria);
```

`new { ... }` creates an **anonymous type**: a quick object, with only the properties you need. `ThenBy` breaks ties: first by total, then by name.

## Deferred execution

A LINQ query **doesn't run** when it is declared, only when it is iterated (by a `foreach`, `ToList()`, `Sum()`...). If you iterate the same query twice, it is computed twice. When you will reuse the result, store it with `.ToList()`.

## Money: use decimal

`double` stores numbers in binary and doesn't represent values like 0.1 exactly: `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. For money, use **`decimal`**, which stores the digits in base 10 and does cent calculations without error. `decimal` literals take the suffix `m` (`1.50m`), and `decimal.Parse(text, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)` reads values with a point.

## LINQ or a loop?

LINQ makes code short and readable, and the same style works for querying databases (Entity Framework) and XML. In a game loop running 60 times per second, however, each query creates new objects; there a simple `for` is usually faster. For data analysis, as in this lesson, LINQ is the right tool.

cs-18.title: Dynamic programming: the change-making problem
cs-18.theory:
# Dynamic programming

In lesson 9, the naive recursive Fibonacci recalculated the same values millions of times. **Dynamic programming** (DP) is the technique of solving a big problem from the answers to **smaller** problems, storing each answer in a table so it is **never computed twice**. It works when the problem has:

1. **optimal substructure**: the best solution is made of the best solutions of subproblems;
2. **overlapping subproblems**: the same pieces show up many times.

## The change-making problem

With coins of given values (as many as you want of each), what is the **smallest number of coins** that adds up exactly to `V`?

The "greedy" idea of always taking the largest coin that fits works with the Brazilian real (1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 cents), but it **fails** in general. With coins `1, 3, 4` and `V = 6`, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 uses only two.

## The table

Let `minimo[v]` be the smallest number of coins to make `v`. Then `minimo[0] = 0` and, for each `v`, we test each coin `m` as "the last coin":

```
minimo[v] = 1 + the smallest of minimo[v - m], for each coin m <= v
```

```csharp
int[] minimo = new int[valor + 1];
Array.Fill(minimo, int.MaxValue);   // "impossible" for now
minimo[0] = 0;
for (int v = 1; v <= valor; v++)
    foreach (int m in moedas)
        if (m <= v && minimo[v - m] != int.MaxValue && minimo[v - m] + 1 < minimo[v])
            minimo[v] = minimo[v - m] + 1;
```

We compute from the bottom up (**bottom-up**): when we reach `v`, all the smaller ones are already done. Cost: **O(V · k)** for `k` coins, instead of exponential.

## Which coins?

The table says **how many**, not **which ones**. To rebuild them, we start from `V` and choose a coin `m` with `minimo[V - m] == minimo[V] - 1` (it leads to an optimal solution), repeating with `V - m`. Always choosing the **largest** coin that works, the result comes out in decreasing order and is always the same.

## Counting the ways

Another question: in **how many ways** can you make `V` (regardless of order)? With `formas[0] = 1`:

```csharp
long[] formas = new long[valor + 1];
formas[0] = 1;
foreach (int m in moedas)              // coin by coin (outer loop!)
    for (int v = m; v <= valor; v++)
        formas[v] += formas[v - m];
```

Putting the coins in the **outer** loop makes each combination count only once ({1, 2} and {2, 1} are the same). Swapping the loops, you would count **sequences** (different orders count separately). Use `long`: the number of ways grows very fast.

## Where DP shows up

Spell checkers (edit distance between words), DNA comparison, the `diff` that shows changes between files, lowest-cost routes, the knapsack problem and image compression. In programming job interviews, DP is one of the most frequent topics.
